Cookie Security Checker

Sends one real HTTP GET request to a URL you choose and classifies the response's Set-Cookie headers into well-documented misconfiguration patterns: SameSite=None missing Secure (rejected outright by current browsers, not just weakened), a __Host-/__Secure- prefixed cookie that violates the attribute rules those prefixes require (also silently rejected), plus notices for a missing Secure attribute, a missing HttpOnly attribute, and no SameSite attribute at all. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test.

1. Run the CLI against your site

Node.js, no dependencies to install:

node check.mjs https://example.com --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you pass; nothing goes through this site.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

Raw Set-Cookie headers

Common questions

What actually happens if a cookie is SameSite=None without Secure?

The browser refuses to set the cookie at all. SameSite=None is how a site opts in to a cookie being sent on cross-site requests -- embedded widgets, cross-site payment flows, federated login -- and the current SameSite specification requires Secure alongside it. Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all enforce that requirement by rejecting the Set-Cookie header outright when Secure is missing, so the failure mode is not a weaker cookie -- the feature the cookie exists for (an embed staying logged in, a cross-site checkout remembering its session) simply breaks, silently, with no error visible to the person who hit it. More background: why a SameSite=None cookie disappears instead of just weakening.

What do the __Host- and __Secure- cookie name prefixes actually enforce?

They are a browser-enforced contract on the cookie's own name, not just documentation. A cookie named __Secure-... must carry the Secure attribute or the browser refuses to store it. A cookie named __Host-... must carry Secure, must not carry a Domain attribute, and must have Path=/ -- again, violate any one of those and the browser refuses to store it. The prefixes exist so that a server can guarantee, just by checking the incoming cookie's name, that it could only have been set by the same secure origin -- a guarantee that is worthless if this portfolio's tool (or any other) only checked the prefix looked right and not that every rule behind it was actually met.

Why is a missing Secure or HttpOnly attribute only a notice, not a danger finding?

Because whether it matters depends on context this tool cannot see from response headers alone. A missing Secure attribute widens exposure to anyone who can observe a future plain-HTTP request to the same host; a missing HttpOnly attribute widens the blast radius of any XSS bug the site might have. Both are real, worth fixing, and reported -- but neither is an unconditional fact about what the browser will do the way SameSite=None-without-Secure and a broken __Host-/__Secure- prefix are, which this tool reserves 'danger' for.

Why can't Set-Cookie headers just be joined into one string and split on commas like other headers?

Because a comma can appear inside a single Set-Cookie header's own value -- the Expires attribute's date format is "Expires=Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT", comma included. Node's http and https clients already know this and expose set-cookie as an array of the individual raw header values rather than folding repeated headers into one comma-joined string the way they do for every other header name. This tool reads that array directly; a naive implementation that reused the comma-join-then-split pattern used for ordinary headers would silently corrupt any cookie carrying an Expires date.

Does a clean report mean the site's cookies have no security issues?

No. This checks a specific, well-documented set of Set-Cookie attribute patterns from one response -- it is not a full security assessment, does not crawl other pages on the site, and cannot see a misconfiguration this tool's checks don't happen to cover (response security headers like CSP and X-Frame-Options are out of scope here -- see security-headers-check for those). Treat a clean report as evidence about these specific patterns, not a determination that the site's cookies are secure.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks a specific, well-documented set of Set-Cookie attribute patterns from one response. It is not a full security assessment, does not crawl other pages on the site, and cannot see a pattern it doesn't check for. A clean report describes what this one request found, not a guarantee the site's cookies are secure.

samesite-none-cookie-rejected.html.text:
Why a SameSite=None cookie disappears instead of just weakening

SameSite=None is how a site opts a cookie in to being sent on cross-site requests -- an embedded widget, a cross-site payment redirect, a federated login flow all depend on it. It is natural to assume that forgetting the accompanying Secure attribute just makes that cookie a little less protected. It does not: the current SameSite specification requires Secure whenever SameSite=None is set, and Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all enforce that by rejecting the Set-Cookie header entirely. No cookie is stored. The feature it existed for -- the embed staying logged in, the payment flow remembering its session -- simply breaks, with nothing in the response that says why.

The same shape applies to __Host- and __Secure-

Cookie name prefixes are usually just a naming convention. These two are not -- they are a contract the browser itself checks before it will store the cookie at all:

PrefixRequired for the browser to store the cookie
__Secure-Secure attribute present
__Host-Secure present, no Domain attribute, Path=/

Miss any one of those rules and the browser silently refuses to store the cookie -- again, no error visible anywhere in the response or the page. A server that checks an incoming __Host-session cookie and trusts that its name alone proves it was set by this exact secure origin is relying on the browser having enforced that when the cookie was created; a malformed Set-Cookie header means that guarantee was never established, and the session simply does not exist rather than existing in some weaker form.

Why this reads as a functional bug before it reads as a security one

Both patterns fail the same way: a person hits the flow, the cookie the server thinks it set is never actually present on the next request, and whatever depended on it -- being logged in, a cart surviving a redirect, a CSRF token matching -- silently stops working. It is usually reported as "login is broken on Safari" or "the checkout redirect logs people out" long before anyone connects it to a missing Secure attribute.

Check your own site automatically

The checker on this site sends one real request, reads every Set-Cookie header exactly as Node's HTTP client already splits them (never joined and re-split on commas, which corrupts a cookie carrying an Expires date), and reports exactly which cookie and which rule triggered a rejection -- plus notices for a missing Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite attribute that weaken a cookie without causing an outright rejection. The request comes from a Node CLI you run yourself against a system you own or are authorised to test; the browser page only renders a report you paste in.

This is evidence from that one response, not a full security assessment -- see the checker and its disclaimer for what it does and doesn't cover.

It is not security advice, and it does not replace a qualified security review or penetration test. vs-cookiebot.html.text:
← Cookie Security Checker

This checker vs. Cookiebot

Cookiebot, from Usercentrics, is one of the best-known cookie consent management platforms. It crawls a site over multiple pages on a schedule, discovers every cookie it can find -- yours and any third party's -- and classifies each one into a consent category (necessary, preferences, statistics, marketing) so the site can show a GDPR/ePrivacy-compliant consent banner and publish an auto-generated cookie declaration page. That is a compliance and disclosure job: which cookies exist, and what is each one for.

This checker does a completely different, much narrower job. It is a single zero-dependency Node CLI: node check.mjs <url> --json sends one request to a URL you choose and reads the response's raw Set-Cookie headers -- not what the cookie is for, but whether it is configured the way current browsers actually require. It flags SameSite=None without Secure (which Chrome, Firefox, and Safari all reject outright, not just weaken), a __Host-/__Secure- prefixed cookie that violates the attribute rules those prefixes demand (also silently rejected), and notices for a missing Secure, missing HttpOnly, or missing SameSite attribute. It has no crawler, no consent-category concept, and no banner -- the browser page here only renders a report from JSON you already have.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Show a GDPR/ePrivacy-compliant consent banner and publish a cookie declaration listing every cookie the site sets and why. Cookiebot -- that is its core product.
Discover cookies set by third-party scripts anywhere on the site, including ones that only appear days into a session. Cookiebot -- continuous multi-page crawling is what finds those.
Know whether a specific cookie's Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite attributes and __Host-/__Secure- prefix are set the way the browser actually requires, so the cookie isn't silently dropped. This checker -- that is the one thing it checks, in detail.
Gate a deploy in your own CI on a SameSite=None-without-Secure or broken-prefix regression, with an exit code, at zero cost. This checker -- node check.mjs <url> exits non-zero on a danger finding.
Get a legally defensible record of consent-category classification for a data protection audit. Cookiebot -- this checker has no concept of consent purpose at all.
Check a single response without an account, a subscription, or any third party's crawler ever touching the site. This checker -- free, local, one request, nothing uploaded.

These compose rather than compete, and a site handling real user data plausibly wants both: Cookiebot for the consent banner and legal disclosure obligation, and this checker wired into CI so a regression in the specific browser-enforced attribute rules it covers turns a build red the day it lands, instead of being noticed later (or never) as cookies quietly failing to persist for some fraction of users. Neither tool replaces the other -- they are not answering the same question.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Cookiebot?

They answer different questions and most sites that need one eventually need both. Cookiebot crawls your site across multiple pages, finds every cookie (yours and any third party's) it can discover, and classifies each one by consent purpose -- necessary, preferences, statistics, marketing -- so you can show a legally compliant consent banner and publish a cookie declaration page, which is a GDPR/ePrivacy compliance job. This checker does not crawl anything and has no concept of consent categories: it sends one request to one URL, reads the raw Set-Cookie header the response actually carries, and reports whether that header is configured the way the current browser specifications require -- SameSite=None with Secure, a __Host-/__Secure- prefix cookie meeting the attribute rules those prefixes demand, Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite present. Reach for Cookiebot to build a consent banner and cookie policy; reach for this to know whether a specific cookie will actually be stored by the browser or silently dropped.

If Cookiebot already lists my site's cookies, why do I also need this?

Because listing a cookie for consent purposes and checking whether the browser will honour its security attributes are unrelated facts about it. Cookiebot's scan tells you a cookie named session exists and which consent category it falls into; it does not tell you that the same cookie is SameSite=None without Secure, which every current major browser rejects outright -- the cookie Cookiebot catalogued for your consent banner may never actually reach the browser's cookie jar at all. This checker reads exactly that: the raw Set-Cookie header, classified against the browser-enforced attribute rules, independent of what the cookie is for.

Why does this need a CLI and a one-page probe instead of crawling the whole site like Cookiebot does?

Because the two tools are solving different-shaped problems. A consent-compliance scan needs to discover every cookie anywhere on the site, including ones set by third-party scripts days into a session, which is why Cookiebot crawls continuously. A Set-Cookie security check is a property of one response at a time -- does this specific header meet the attribute rules the browser enforces -- so a single request against the endpoint you care about is enough to answer it, and a small local CLI you run yourself (or wire into CI) answers it without a subscription, an account, or a third party's crawler ever touching your site.

Is Cookiebot free like this checker?

Cookiebot offers a free tier for a single domain with usage limits, alongside paid plans for more domains, more page scans, and consent-management features -- see Cookiebot's own site for current pricing and limits, which this page does not track. This checker is free and open source under an MIT licence with no tiers, no account, and no usage limits of its own; being free is not really the distinguishing question here, though -- the tools check different things regardless of price.

Is this page affiliated with Cookiebot or Usercentrics?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Cookiebot or its parent company Usercentrics, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. What Cookiebot currently scans and how its consent platform works are described on its own site -- check there for what it covers today.

Only point either tool at a system you own or are authorised to test. That rule is unchanged by which one you pick.

← Back to the checker

Evidence, not a determination. This checker looks at a specific, well-documented set of Set-Cookie attribute patterns from one response. It is not a full security assessment, does not crawl other pages on the site, and cannot see a pattern its checks don't happen to cover. A clean report describes what this one request found, not a guarantee the site's cookies are secure.

vs-curl-and-reading-headers-yourself.htm.text:
← Cookie Security Checker

This checker vs. curl -I and reading the headers yourself

curl -I https://example.com/ gets you the raw Set-Cookie header text in seconds, and for a quick look that's often all you need. The value this tool adds isn't reading the attribute names -- curl already shows you those. It's two things a manual read (or a naive script built on top of curl's output) gets wrong.

First, knowing which attribute combinations a browser actively rejects rather than merely tolerates weakened. SameSite=None without Secure, and a __Host- or __Secure- prefixed cookie that violates the attribute rules those prefixes require, aren't read as "less secure" by Chrome, Firefox, and Safari -- they're rejected outright, and the cookie is never stored at all. Nothing about the raw header text tells you that; you have to already know the rejection rules and apply them yourself, attribute combination by attribute combination.

Second, parsing repeated Set-Cookie headers correctly. Most response headers that repeat can be joined into one string and split on commas. Set-Cookie cannot: an Expires attribute carries a comma of its own (Expires=Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT), so that join-then-split silently corrupts any cookie that sets one. This tool reads each Set-Cookie header as its own separate value -- the way Node's own HTTP client already hands them back -- and never rejoins or re-splits them.

A worked example of the corruption

Two real Set-Cookie headers from one response:

#Header value
1session=abc123; Path=/; Expires=Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT; Secure; HttpOnly
2csrf=xyz789; SameSite=None
Read correctly (this checker)Joined and split on commas (the naive shortcut)
2 cookies: session (Path, Expires, Secure, HttpOnly) and csrf (SameSite=None, flagged samesite-none-without-secure). 3 fragments: session=abc123; Path=/; Expires=Wed, then 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT; Secure; HttpOnly with no cookie name attached at all, then csrf=xyz789; SameSite=None.

The Expires attribute's own comma splits the session cookie's value away from its trailing attributes mid-string, turning two real cookies into three fragments and leaving one of them with no name at all. A tool built on the join-then-split shortcut either drops that fragment or misreports it -- either way, it never reaches the actual attributes it was supposed to check.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I just want to eyeball whether a cookie has Secure or HttpOnly set at all. curl -I -- that's exactly its job, and this tool checks the same attributes as a stricter, automated pass.
I want to know whether an attribute combination is one a browser actively rejects, not just weaker. This checker -- applies the SameSite=None/Secure rule and the __Host-/__Secure- prefix contract for you, instead of leaving you to know and re-check both by eye.
I want this checked automatically in CI against my own staging environment. node check.mjs <url> -- exit code 1 on a danger-severity finding, no reading required.
I'm scripting my own parser on top of curl's output and it needs to handle multiple Set-Cookie headers. This checker's parseSetCookieHeader -- or at minimum, don't join repeated headers into one string before splitting on commas.

Common questions

Isn't curl -I enough to see a site's Set-Cookie headers?

curl -I shows you the raw header text, which is the easy part. What it doesn't tell you is which attribute combinations a compliant browser actively rejects rather than merely tolerates weakened -- SameSite=None without Secure, or a __Host-/__Secure- prefix whose attribute rules aren't met. Reading three attribute names off a terminal doesn't carry that judgment with it; you have to already know the rejection rules to apply them by eye.

What goes wrong if I script this myself against curl's output?

The common shortcut is joining every Set-Cookie header into one string and splitting it on commas, the way most other repeated response headers can be handled. Set-Cookie can't: an Expires attribute contains its own comma ("Expires=Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT"), so that join-then-split silently breaks into the wrong number of fragments and corrupts the cookie's attributes the moment one of them carries an Expires date.

Can you show a real example of the corruption?

Two Set-Cookie headers: a session cookie with Path, Expires, Secure, and HttpOnly, and a csrf cookie with SameSite=None. Correctly read as two separate header values, that's two cookies. Joined with ", " and split on every comma instead, the Expires date's own comma splits the session cookie's attributes away from its name mid-value, producing three fragments instead of two -- one of which is just "21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT; Secure; HttpOnly" with no cookie name attached to it at all.

Is my target URL or its cookies uploaded anywhere?

No. The CLI (check.mjs) sends its one request straight from your machine to the URL you name -- never through this site. The browser page only parses JSON you paste into it yourself, locally. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day, with no target URLs and no Set-Cookie values in it.

Want the fuller explanation of why the SameSite/prefix rejections read as functional bugs before they read as security ones? Read why a SameSite=None cookie disappears instead of just weakening.

It is not a full security assessment, does not crawl other pages on the site, and cannot see a pattern its checks don't happen to cover. A clean report describes what this one request found, not a guarantee the site's cookies are secure.
